Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI last month, accusing the company behind ChatGPT of stealing trade secrets related to hardware development. Nearly a month later, OpenAI published a blog post responding in detail to many of Apple's allegations.

First, let me briefly recap the timeline of events:

  • July 10: Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing former Apple employees of systematically stealing Apple's trade secrets to benefit OpenAI's future hardware business.
  • July 10: OpenAI issued a brief statement in response: "We have no interest in any other company's trade secrets. We will remain focused on developing innovative technologies that empower users around the world."
  • July 14: OpenAI issued an updated response, stating that it had not seen any evidence to support Apple's allegations.

Moving to August 4, OpenAI published a blog post late that night, finally providing a more detailed response. You can read the full text here.

The article was titled "Apple Got It Wrong" and was published under OpenAI's name.

OpenAI's latest response begins by characterizing the lawsuit as "reckless, aggressive, and unusually targeted":

Next, OpenAI appears to suggest that it was not properly notified of the issues before the lawsuit was filed, including some details that had already been reported prior to today:

They then provided email correspondence records that can be viewed on the web.

Then, the response finally acknowledged some of the data access issues raised by Apple:

If you have read Apple's initial lawsuit documents, you would know that Tang Tan is the main focus of the complaint. OpenAI's response tonight defended him:

The remainder of the response contains only two more paragraphs before transitioning to screenshots of email and iMessage conversations. Here is the concluding section:

We wish Apple had communicated with us about these issues before filing the lawsuit, as we would have been happy to clarify everything for them. We have taken the allegations in the lawsuit seriously and have offered to work with Apple to resolve them. However, they are attempting to rewrite the narrative, including making vague accusations against other former employees, and are likely to continue doing so. Apple's basis for seeking a temporary injunction is based on misinformation and is entirely unnecessary, as we neither have nor want any of their trade secrets. What we are more interested in is building innovative products and technologies that push the frontier forward.

That is roughly the current situation. This is not an official legal response, but in the three and a half weeks since Apple initially filed the lawsuit, this is the most OpenAI has said (or shown).

As a reminder, you can read OpenAI's new response here and view Apple's original complaint here.
